title: Logistic Regression III - Log Loss and Maximum Likelihood
abstract:
The final piece. The perceptron gave a boundary and the sigmoid gave a
probability, but neither told us which weights are best. Maximum likelihood
does: choose the parameters that make the observed labels most probable. This
document derives the likelihood, takes its logarithm to obtain log loss, proves
the loss is convex (so gradient descent always finds the global optimum), derives
the gradient and shows why it takes the same form as linear regression's, and
covers the practical issues — numerical stability, perfect separation, and why
squared error is the wrong loss here.

blocks.t: The Problem
From the notes
With perceptron & sigmoid, still not the best output.

Crux — in ML we look for a loss function / error function. The difference
of predicted and actual, by a formula. After we know the formula we find the
minima, and the coefficients over there are the actual good solution.
That paragraph is the recipe for essentially every model in this course:

items: Write down a formula measuring how wrong the predictions are.
Find the parameters that minimise it.
Those parameters are the model.

blocks.t:
The perceptron had no such formula — only a rule that reacted to mistakes. That
is why it could not say which of two separating lines was better, and why it never
terminated on overlapping data.
From Likelihood to Log Loss
Step 1 — the probability of one observation

The model outputs $p_i=\sigma(w^{\!\top}x_i+b)=P(y_i=1\mid x_i)$. The probability
of actually observing the label $y_i\in\{0,1\}$ is

The compact form is a standard trick: when $y_i=1$ the second factor is
$(1-p_i)^0=1$; when $y_i=0$ the first is $p_i^0=1$. One expression, both cases.
Step 2 — the likelihood of the whole dataset
Assuming the observations are independent, multiply:
\mathcal{L}(w,b)=\prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i^{ y_i}\left(1-p_i\right)^{1-y_i} .

Maximum likelihood says: choose $w$ and $b$ to make this as large as
possible — i.e. to make the labels we actually saw as probable as possible
under the model.

blocks.cap:
Left: the likelihood is a product of $n$ numbers less than 1, so for
 even 60 observations it is around $10^{-18}$ — and for a real dataset it
 underflows to exactly zero. Right: taking the negative logarithm turns the
 product into a sum, which is numerically stable and has the same optimum.

blocks.t: Step 3 — take the logarithm

$\log$ is strictly increasing, so maximising $\mathcal L$ is the same as
maximising $\log\mathcal L$. And $\log$ turns products into sums:
\log\mathcal{L}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big[y_i\log p_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\Big].
By convention we minimise rather than maximise, so negate and average:

This is also called binary cross-entropy. Maximising likelihood and
minimising log loss are the same operation.
Reading the formula
For each observation exactly one term survives:

items:
$y_i=1$: the loss is $-\log(p_i)$. Predict $p=0.99$ and pay $0.01$;
 predict $p=0.01$ and pay $4.6$.
$y_i=0$: the loss is $-\log(1-p_i)$, mirrored.

blocks.t:
As $p\to0$ with $y=1$, the loss $\to\infty$. Being confidently wrong is
punished without bound, which is precisely the behaviour you want from a model
that outputs probabilities.

blocks.cap:
Left: the two branches of the log loss. Middle: squared error is
 bounded — predicting $0.01$ when the truth is 1 costs only $0.98$, so the
 model is barely penalised for being certain and wrong. Right: convexity.

blocks.t: Why Not Squared Error?

head: Log loss
Squared error
rows: MLE for Gaussian — the wrong distribution
Contains an extra $\sigma'$ factor that vanishes in the tails

blocks.t: The gradient argument is the decisive one

With squared error the gradient carries a factor $\sigma'(z)=\sigma(1-\sigma)$,
which is near zero when the model is confidently wrong — exactly when you most
need a large update. The model gets stuck. Log loss's gradient contains no
such factor: the $\sigma'$ from the chain rule cancels exactly against the
$1/p$ from the logarithm. That cancellation is not luck — it is why the pairing
of sigmoid with cross-entropy is standard everywhere in machine learning.
The Gradient
Deriving it, and watching the cancellation

Take one observation with $z=w^{\!\top}x+b$ and $p=\sigma(z)$. The loss is
$\ell=-\left[y\log p+(1-y)\log(1-p)\right]$.
From Topic 45, $\dfrac{\partial p}{\partial z}=p(1-p)$. Chain rule:
The $p(1-p)$ terms cancel exactly. Then $\partial z/\partial w=x$, giving
Compare with linear regression

\text{Linear regression:}\quad \nabla_w L=\frac{2}{n}X^{ \top}\left(Xw-y\right)
 \qquad
 \text{Logistic:}\quad \nabla_w L=\frac{1}{n}X^{ \top}\left(\sigma(Xw)-y\right)

Identical in form — $X^{\!\top}$ times the error — with the only
difference being that the prediction passes through a sigmoid. Every technique
from Topics 37–38 (batch, stochastic, mini-batch, learning rates, scaling)
transfers unchanged.

blocks.cap:
Gradient descent on the log loss. The surface is a convex bowl, so
 every starting point reaches the same global minimum, and the loss falls
 monotonically.

blocks.t: Proof of convexity
The Hessian is

H=\frac{1}{n}X^{ \top}SX,
 \qquad S=\operatorname{diag} \big(p_i(1-p_i)\big).

Since $0<p_i<1$, every diagonal entry of $S$ is strictly positive. For any vector
$v$,
v^{ \top}Hv=\frac1n (Xv)^{ \top}S(Xv)=\frac1n\sum_i p_i(1-p_i)(Xv)_i^{2} \ge 0 .

So $H$ is positive semi-definite and the loss is convex. There are no
local minima — any stationary point is the global optimum.

There is no closed form, however: setting $X^{\!\top}(\sigma(Xw)-y)=0$ gives a
system that is non-linear in $w$ because of the sigmoid. Hence the iterative
solution.
The Full Algorithm
The steps, from the notes

items: Start with input data.
Assume a linear equation.
Convert to probability using the sigmoid.
Calculate loss (log loss).
Update weights/coefficients using gradient descent.

Stop training if max iteration is reached or loss stops
 decreasing.
Make the final prediction: $P\ge0.5\Rightarrow1$, else $0$.

blocks.t:
Note: the sigmoid alone didn't tell us the best weights, so we used
gradient descent to find them.
Practical Issues
Numerical stability

$\log(0)=-\infty$. If the model outputs exactly $0$ or $1$ — which happens with
float64 once $|z|\gtrsim37$ — the loss becomes inf or nan. Two
fixes:

items:
Clip: $p\leftarrow\operatorname{clip}(p,\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon)$ with
 $\varepsilon=10^{-15}$. This is what sklearn.metrics.log_loss does.

Better: compute the loss directly from $z$ using the log-sum-exp form
 $\ell = \max(z,0)-zy+\log\!\left(1+e^{-|z|}\right)$, which never
 exponentiates a large positive number.

blocks.t: Perfect separation makes the weights diverge

If the classes are perfectly separable, the likelihood can always be increased by
scaling $w$ up: doubling $w$ pushes every $p_i$ closer to 0 or 1 and reduces the
loss further. The maximum likelihood estimate is at infinity — the
optimiser never converges and the coefficients grow without bound.

Symptoms: a ConvergenceWarning, coefficients in the hundreds, and
probabilities that are all $0.000$ or $1.000$. The fix is regularisation, which is
why scikit-learn applies $L_2$ by default (Topic 52). This is also the
reason logistic regression, unlike the perceptron, needs no separability
assumption — and is in fact troubled by too much of it.
Code

import numpy as np
from scipy.special import expit
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import log_loss
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 400
X = np.c_[rng.normal(0, 1, n), rng.normal(0, 1, n)]
z_true = 2.0 * X[:, 0] - 1.5 * X[:, 1] + 0.5
y = (rng.random(n) < expit(z_true)).astype(int)

# =====================================================================
# 1. THE COMPACT LIKELIHOOD TRICK
# =====================================================================
p = np.array([0.9, 0.9, 0.2, 0.2])
lab = np.array([1, 0, 1, 0])
print("p^y * (1-p)^(1-y):", (p**lab * (1-p)**(1-lab)).round(4))
print("what it should be :", [0.9, 0.1, 0.2, 0.8])
# One expression handles both cases, because x^0 = 1.

# =====================================================================
# 2. WHY WE TAKE THE LOG -- the product underflows
# =====================================================================
w_true = np.array([2.0, -1.5, 0.5])
Xb = np.c_[X, np.ones(n)]
pp = expit(Xb @ w_true)

likelihood = np.prod(pp**y * (1-pp)**(1-y))
print(f"\nlikelihood of {n} observations: {likelihood:.3e}")
big = np.prod(np.r_[pp, pp, pp, pp, pp]**np.r_[y,y,y,y,y] *
              (1-np.r_[pp,pp,pp,pp,pp])**(1-np.r_[y,y,y,y,y]))
print(f"with 2000 observations:        {big:.3e}   <- UNDERFLOWED to 0")

loglik = np.sum(y*np.log(pp) + (1-y)*np.log(1-pp))
print(f"log-likelihood (a SUM):        {loglik:.4f}   <- perfectly fine")

# =====================================================================
# 3. LOG LOSS, FROM SCRATCH
# =====================================================================
def log_loss_scratch(y, p, eps=1e-15):
    p = np.clip(p, eps, 1 - eps)                    # log(0) = -inf otherwise
    return -np.mean(y*np.log(p) + (1-y)*np.log(1-p))

print(f"\nscratch log loss: {log_loss_scratch(y, pp):.6f}")
print(f"sklearn log loss: {log_loss(y, pp):.6f}")

# The numerically STABLE form, computed straight from z:
def log_loss_from_z(y, z):
    """max(z,0) - z*y + log(1 + exp(-|z|))  -- never overflows."""
    return np.mean(np.maximum(z, 0) - z*y + np.log1p(np.exp(-np.abs(z))))

print(f"stable form     : {log_loss_from_z(y, Xb @ w_true):.6f}")
print("naive form on z = -1000:", end=" ")
try:
    with np.errstate(over="raise", divide="raise"):
        print(log_loss_scratch(np.array([1]), expit(np.array([-1000.]))))
except Exception:
    print("clipped to 34.54 (information lost)")
print("stable form on z = -1000:", round(log_loss_from_z(np.array([1]),
                                                         np.array([-1000.])), 2))

# =====================================================================
# 4. CONFIDENTLY WRONG COSTS AN UNBOUNDED AMOUNT
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'y':>3s} {'p':>8s} {'log loss':>10s} {'squared err':>12s}")
for yi, pi in [(1, 0.99), (1, 0.60), (1, 0.50), (1, 0.10), (1, 0.01), (1, 1e-6)]:
    print(f"{yi:3d} {pi:8.4g} {-np.log(pi):10.4f} {(yi-pi)**2:12.4f}")
# Log loss explodes; squared error is capped at 1.0 and barely reacts.

# =====================================================================
# 5. THE GRADIENT -- and the exact cancellation
# =====================================================================
def gradient(w, X, y):
    p = expit(X @ w)
    return X.T @ (p - y) / len(y)                   # (1/n) X'(sigma(Xw) - y)

w0 = np.array([0.4, -0.2, 0.1])
an = gradient(w0, Xb, y)

eps = 1e-6                                          # numerical check
num = np.array([(log_loss_from_z(y, Xb @ (w0 + eps*e)) -
                 log_loss_from_z(y, Xb @ (w0 - eps*e))) / (2*eps)
                for e in np.eye(3)])
print(f"\nanalytic gradient: {an.round(8)}")
print(f"numeric  gradient: {num.round(8)}")
print(f"max difference   : {np.abs(an-num).max():.2e}")

# The cancellation, shown term by term for one observation:
i = 0
zi, pi, yi = Xb[i] @ w0, expit(Xb[i] @ w0), y[i]
dl_dp = -yi/pi + (1-yi)/(1-pi)                      # = (p - y) / (p(1-p))
dp_dz = pi * (1 - pi)                               # sigma'
print(f"\ndl/dp = {dl_dp:.6f}   dp/dz = {dp_dz:.6f}")
print(f"product = {dl_dp*dp_dz:.6f}   and (p - y) = {pi-yi:.6f}   <- identical")

# =====================================================================
# 6. GRADIENT DESCENT, EXACTLY AS THE NOTES DESCRIBE
# =====================================================================
def fit_logistic(X, y, lr=0.5, max_iter=5000, tol=1e-8):
    Xb = np.c_[X, np.ones(len(X))]                  # 1. input data
    w = np.zeros(Xb.shape[1])                       # 2. assume a linear equation
    prev = np.inf
    for it in range(max_iter):
        z = Xb @ w
        p = expit(z)                                # 3. convert to probability
        loss = log_loss_from_z(y, z)                # 4. calculate log loss
        w -= lr * (Xb.T @ (p - y) / len(y))         # 5. gradient descent update
        if abs(prev - loss) < tol:                  # 6. stop when loss plateaus
            return w, it, loss
        prev = loss
    return w, max_iter, prev

w_hat, iters, final = fit_logistic(X, y)
print(f"\nconverged in {iters} iterations, log loss {final:.6f}")
print(f"scratch weights: {w_hat.round(4)}")
print(f"true weights   : {w_true.round(4)}")

sk = LogisticRegression(penalty=None, max_iter=5000).fit(X, y)
print(f"sklearn        : {np.r_[sk.coef_[0], sk.intercept_].round(4)}")

# 7. make the final prediction
probs = expit(np.c_[X, np.ones(n)] @ w_hat)
pred  = (probs >= 0.5).astype(int)
print(f"accuracy: {(pred == y).mean():.4f}   matches sklearn: "
      f"{np.array_equal(pred, sk.predict(X))}")

# =====================================================================
# 7. CONVEXITY -- every starting point reaches the same answer
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'start':>26s} {'final weights':>34s}")
for start in [np.zeros(3), np.array([10., -10., 5.]), rng.normal(0, 5, 3)]:
    w = start.copy()
    for _ in range(6000):
        w -= 0.5 * gradient(w, Xb, y)
    print(f"{np.array2string(start, precision=1):>26s} "
          f"{np.array2string(w, precision=4):>34s}")
# Identical, because the loss is convex.

# The Hessian is PSD -- verify it:
pv = expit(Xb @ w_hat)
H = Xb.T @ np.diag(pv*(1-pv)) @ Xb / n
print(f"\nHessian eigenvalues all >= 0: {(np.linalg.eigvalsh(H) >= -1e-12).all()}")
print(f"eigenvalues: {np.linalg.eigvalsh(H).round(4)}")

# =====================================================================
# 8. WHY SQUARED ERROR FAILS -- the gradient vanishes when confidently wrong
# =====================================================================
def grad_mse(w, X, y):
    p = expit(X @ w)
    return X.T @ ((p - y) * p * (1 - p)) / len(y)   # note the EXTRA sigma' factor

w_bad = np.array([-8.0, 6.0, 0.0])                  # deliberately very wrong
print(f"\nat badly wrong weights:")
print(f"  log loss gradient norm: {np.linalg.norm(gradient(w_bad, Xb, y)):.6f}")
print(f"  MSE      gradient norm: {np.linalg.norm(grad_mse(w_bad, Xb, y)):.6f}")
# The MSE gradient is far smaller -- the model is stuck exactly where it most
# needs to move. The sigma(1-sigma) factor is ~0 for confident predictions.

# =====================================================================
# 9. PERFECT SEPARATION -- the MLE runs off to infinity
# =====================================================================
Xs = np.array([[1.], [2.], [3.], [8.], [9.], [10.]])
ys = np.array([0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1])                   # perfectly separable

import warnings
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
    for C in [1e10, 1.0, 0.01]:
        m = LogisticRegression(C=C, max_iter=10000).fit(Xs, ys)
        print(f"C={C:<8g} coef {m.coef_[0][0]:10.3f}  "
              f"P at x=3: {m.predict_proba([[3.]])[0,1]:.6f}")
# With no regularisation the coefficient explodes and probabilities saturate.
# Regularisation is what keeps it finite -- which is why sklearn applies L2
# by DEFAULT (Topic 52).

blocks.t: Why not squared error. Squared error on probabilities is bounded by 1, so a confident mistake costs at most 1. Log loss grows without bound as $p \to 0$ for a true positive, which is what pushes the optimiser away from confident errors.

The gradient is simple. With $z$ the linear score and $p=\sigma(z)$, $\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial z} = p - y$. For the first row: $0.9 - 1 = -0.1$, so the update raises $z$ by a small amount. For the second row: $0.1 - 1 = -0.9$, a large push. Error size drives the step, exactly as in linear regression.
Link to maximum likelihood. Minimising the average log loss is the same as maximising the likelihood of the labels under a Bernoulli model with probability $p$.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
With perceptron & sigmoid, still not the best output. We need a
 loss function: a formula for the difference between predicted and
 actual, whose minima give the good coefficients.

The probability of one observation is $p_i^{y_i}(1-p_i)^{1-y_i}$; the
 likelihood of the dataset is their product.

Taking $-\log$ turns the product into a sum and gives
 $$\text{Log Loss}=-\frac1n\sum_i\left[y_i\log p_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\right],$$
 also called binary cross-entropy. Maximising likelihood $=$ minimising log
 loss.

Being confidently wrong costs an unbounded amount —
 $-\log p\to\infty$ as $p\to0$.

Squared error is wrong here: it is non-convex in $w$, it barely penalises
 confident mistakes, and its gradient carries a $\sigma'$ factor that
 vanishes exactly when the model is most wrong.

The gradient is $\nabla_w L=\frac1n X^{\!\top}(\sigma(Xw)-y)$ — the
 $\sigma'$ from the chain rule cancels against the $1/p$ from the log.
 Identical in form to linear regression's.

The Hessian $\frac1n X^{\!\top}SX$ is positive semi-definite, so the loss
 is convex — one global minimum, reachable from any start. There
 is no closed form, so it is solved iteratively.

The algorithm: input $\to$ linear equation $\to$ sigmoid $\to$
 log loss $\to$ gradient descent $\to$ stop on max iterations or plateau
 $\to$ predict with $P\ge0.5$.

Watch for numerical overflow, and for perfect separation, where
 the MLE diverges and regularisation becomes mandatory.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Derive the log loss.

The probability of one label is $p^y(1-p)^{1-y}$. The likelihood of the dataset is
the product over observations. Take the logarithm to convert it into a sum, negate
to make it a minimisation, and average — giving
$-\frac1n\sum[y\log p+(1-y)\log(1-p)]$.
Q. Why take the log at all?

Two reasons. Numerically, the product of thousands of numbers below 1 underflows
to zero, whereas a sum of logarithms does not. Mathematically, sums are far easier
to differentiate than products. And since $\log$ is monotonic, the maximiser is
unchanged.
Q. Why not use MSE for logistic regression?

Three reasons. It is non-convex in the weights, so gradient descent can stall in a
local minimum. It barely penalises confident mistakes — predicting $0.01$ when
the truth is 1 costs under 1.0. And its gradient carries a $\sigma(1-\sigma)$
factor that goes to zero exactly when the model is most confidently wrong, so
learning stops. Log loss's gradient has no such factor.
Q. What is the gradient of the log loss?

$\frac1n X^{\!\top}(\sigma(Xw)-y)$ — $X^{\!\top}$ times the prediction error.
It has the same form as linear regression's gradient; the only difference is that
the prediction passes through a sigmoid. The $\sigma'$ from the chain rule cancels
exactly against the $1/p$ from the logarithm.
Q. Is the logistic loss convex? Is there a closed form?

Convex yes — the Hessian $\frac1n X^{\!\top}SX$ with
$S=\operatorname{diag}(p_i(1-p_i))$ is positive semi-definite, so any stationary
point is global. Closed form no — setting the gradient to zero gives a system
that is non-linear in $w$ because of the sigmoid, so it is solved iteratively.

Q. Your logistic regression reports a convergence warning and huge
coefficients. Why?

Perfect (or near-perfect) separation. The likelihood always improves by scaling
$w$ up, so the maximum likelihood estimate is at infinity. Add regularisation —
which is why scikit-learn applies $L_2$ by default.
Q. What does it mean that log loss is the negative log-likelihood?

That minimising it is exactly maximum likelihood estimation under a Bernoulli
model. The same relationship holds for linear regression with squared error under
a Gaussian model — which is why each loss goes with its own output distribution.
